headings.title: Introduction and Clinical Importance of the Foetal Skull
headings.content: The foetal skull is the largest and least compressible part of the baby. Its anatomy directly dictates how a baby navigates the maternal pelvis during childbirth. Midwives and obstetricians study this structure closely because many labour complications arise from a mismatch between the size of the foetal head and the birth canal. Unlike the adult skull, the foetal head features flexible plates joined by membranes. This design protects delicate brain tissue while allowing the bones to overlap during passage through the tight pelvic brim.

headings.title: Bones of the Foetal Skull
headings.content:
The vault of the foetal skull consists of several distinct flat bones that are not yet fused together. 

- **Frontal bones**: Two distinct bones at the front that eventually fuse after birth to form the forehead.
- **Parietal bones**: Two large bones forming the sides and roof of the cranium, meeting at the sagittal suture.
- **Occipital bone**: A single bone at the back of the head that forms the base of the skull.
- **Temporal bones**: Two bones situated on the lower sides of the skull near the ears.

headings.title: Sutures of the Foetal Skull
headings.content:
Sutures are membrane-filled spaces that separate the cranial bones. They provide flexibility and serve as vital anatomical landmarks during vaginal examinations in labour. 

- **Sagittal suture**: Runs down the midline, separating the two parietal bones.
- **Coronal suture**: Separates the frontal bones from the parietal bones.
- **Lambdoid suture**: Separates the occipital bone from the two parietal bones.
- **Frontal suture**: Runs between the two unmerged halves of the frontal bone.

headings.title: Fontanelles and Their Clinical Significance
headings.content:
Fontanelles are wider membranous spaces where multiple sutures intersect. The two main fontanelles assessed during obstetric care are the anterior and posterior fontanelles.

- **Anterior fontanelle (Bregma)**: Diamond-shaped, formed by the meeting of the sagittal, coronal, and frontal sutures. It remains open until about 18 months after birth.
- **Posterior fontanelle (Lambda)**: Triangular-shaped, formed by the junction of the sagittal and lambdoid sutures. It usually closes much earlier, around six to eight weeks postpartum.

Clinically, a sunken fontanelle can indicate dehydration, while a bulging fontanelle may signal increased intracranial pressure.

headings.title: Regions and Landmarks of the Foetal Skull
headings.content:
For descriptive purposes, the foetal skull is divided into specific regions that help healthcare providers document foetal presentation and engagement accurately. 

- **Vertex**: The area bounded by the two parietal eminences and the posterior fontanelle. This is the presenting part in the most common and favorable delivery position.
- **Face**: The area extending from the root of the nose to the orbital ridges and chin.
- **Brow (Synciput)**: The area between the root of the nose and the anterior fontanelle.
- **Occiput**: The area overlying the occipital bone, behind the posterior fontanelle.

headings.title: Diameters of the Foetal Skull
headings.content:
The transverse and anteroposterior diameters of the foetal skull dictate how easily the head passes through the pelvis. When the head is well-flexed, it presents a smaller diameter, making labour progress smoothly. 

| Diameter | Extent | Measurement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Suboccipito-bregmatic | From beneath the occiput to the centre of the anterior fontanelle | 9.5 cm |
| Occipito-frontalis | From the bridge of the nose to the posterior fontanelle | 11.5 cm |
| Mento-vertical | From the chin to the highest point of the vertex | 13.5 cm |
| Submento-bregmatic | From below the chin to the center of the anterior fontanelle | 9.5 cm |

An unflexed head presents larger diameters like the occipito-frontalis or mento-vertical, which often lead to obstructed labour.

headings.title: Moulding of the Foetal Skull During Labour
headings.content: Moulding is the natural shifting and overlapping of the cranial bones along the sutures as the foetal head endures uterine contractions and maternal pushing. This adaptation reduces the skull's dimensions without harming the brain, provided the process is gradual and within physiological limits. Excessive or rapid moulding can cause intracranial haemorrhage or tearing of bridging veins. Midwives assess moulding during vaginal examinations to monitor the progress of labour and detect disproportion early.
